title: From Stateless Nightmares to Durable Agents — Samuel Colvin, Pydantic
talk_summary: Samuel Colvin demos wrapping Pydantic AI agents in Temporal so every LLM call and tool call becomes a recorded activity, letting long agent runs resume after crashes and replay completed steps instantly from cached results. He also shows a multi-agent deep-research pipeline (plan agent, parallel search agents via task group, analysis agent) and briefly notes evals revealed a cheaper/faster model was just inventing wrong answers.

takeaways.what_they_do: Wrap each agent so all LLM and tool IO becomes a Temporal activity; the workflow stays deterministic and Temporal records inputs/outputs of every activity, so a killed process resumes and replays finished steps from cache instead of re-calling the model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Temporal just returned the result, the kind of cached result that it already had for each of these cases.
takeaways.numbers: Replayed plan step took 24ms; earlier LLM calls returned in ~5ms on resume

takeaways.what_they_do: He stresses that durability is only useful if tool calls (not just LLM calls) are activities, so side-effecting steps are recorded and not re-executed on replay.
takeaways.evidence_quote: OpenAI claim to have temporal support, but they don't support tool calls as activities, which to me makes it slightly a chocolate teapot.

takeaways.technique: Imperative parallel fan-out with task groups
takeaways.what_they_do: Deep-research pipeline runs a plan agent, then fans out N search agents in parallel with a plain Python task group, then feeds all results as XML into a final analysis agent — no graph framework needed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: We run in parallel all of the search agents. So, we're just using a task group from Python to run all of these.
takeaways.numbers: Up to 5-10 parallel searches; run cost ~8 cents mid-run

takeaways.what_they_do: Ran Pydantic evals across models tracking pass/fail assertions, average cost, and steps-to-success; discovered the cheapest/fastest model was fast because it fabricated answers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the reason Gemini is way faster and answers much more quickly is it just invents an answer that's wrong and I wasn't checking it.
takeaways.numbers: Gemini 'way way cheaper, way way faster' but wrong; up to 46 steps without success

takeaways.what_they_do: Uses a small/fast model for the answer agent and search agents, and a stronger model (Claude Sonnet) only for the final analysis stage.

takeaways.technique: Long activity timeouts for slow steps
takeaways.what_they_do: Gave the long analysis activity an hour timeout instead of the default ~2 minutes so it wouldn't fail mid-run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I give it I think it was taking longer than 2 minutes or whatever the default is. So I just gave it an hour so it's not going to fail.
